P1.evidence: Full four-part frame delivered cleanly: 'where you are today, where you want to get to, what's been getting in the way, what you genuinely need to get there. So we look at it as kind of like a transformation conversation.' Open question asked: 'walk me through what we potentially help you with.' P1a is partial because the read-back was a bare gesture — 'So I went through. So I have a bit of a head start' — with no specific detail returned to the prospect, so nothing about it made him feel seen. P1c is partial because frame agreement was asserted rather than asked: the rep said 'That'll work for you' as a statement. He did get assent ('That's great. That's great.') but the check is a question and it was not one.

P2.evidence: Training history was covered exceptionally well and the basics were skipped. P2a is a miss under the rule that volunteered information does not count: age, height and weight all appeared inside the prospect's opening monologue — 'I'm going to be 60 this year', 'I'm 5'10 ish, five, a little bit more than 5'10. And I weigh 182' — and the rep never asked for any of them. P2b hit: 'work-wise, are we sitting all day, or what's that look like?' P2c and P2d were asked as one compound question — 'What about like health conditions, injuries, chronic pain, anything that limits movement?' — which is efficient but left hereditary conditions unasked and, more importantly, drew no follow-up. The answer 'No, no issues' was accepted, the volunteered history of back problems got 'Okay, nice', and the shoulder mobility restriction the prospect raised minutes later was never connected back. P2e is a clear hit with three separate questions on training days, kettlebell frequency and other modalities. P2f hit — the plateau was explored properly. P2g hit. P2h and P2i are partial because sleep and energy were compressed into one question, the answer covered only sleep hours, and energy was never actually answered.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals phase in the batch. P3a asked directly: 'are we pretty content with where the physique is as a whole right now, or how are we feeling in that?' P3b asked as a genuine open sweep: 'outside of the increased weight, what about, like, mobility, aesthetics, conditioning, like, is there any other goals?' — which is what surfaced the shoulder mobility and the Turkish get-up ceiling. P3c landed through the six-month target question and produced a precise, testable answer: 26 kg doubles overhead. P3d was asked twice and pushed the second time — 'what's the drive behind, you know, having more muscle longevity, staying away from, like, why are we, why are we doing it?' P3h is a real reflect-back, the only one in the batch: 'I kind of get the sense that there's a really big desire to like master this at like, like at the highest level you can. Is that what I'm understanding? Is that a fair statement?' answered 'Yeah... it is a question of mastering it.' Where it falls short: P3e was replaced by the devil's-advocate challenge rather than asked, so the prospect never described what the improvement would give him. P3f was never asked at all — this man has a wife and a son and neither was explored for a single question. P3g reached longevity and identity but nothing on family or legacy, which is the same shape of gap the rep shows on every call in this batch.

P4.evidence: Also the strongest P4 in the batch, and notable because it is exactly what the rep failed to do on the Tom Eldon call the same day. P4a asked: 'Is there anything else outside of that you've been trying to improve on kettlebells?' and 'how long have been doing that kettlebell stuff for?' P4b asked and produced the whole arc: 'What did change? Because I know you've been saying you've been kind of getting bored of the workouts, but it's also, I mean, six years is a long time to do stuff' — which surfaced the pre-COVID gym work with Kelvin Gary, the shift to training alone, and the staleness. P4f ran in substance and was the best move on the call, a direct challenge to the prospect's own premise: 'we're talking about, you know, because you can do that with what you've been doing now, right? But now we're talking about getting to the next level. So why the next level versus just kind of plateauing? Because you can get a lot of those benefits from just doing what you're doing now.' That is the right question and it forced a real answer. P4e hit — the prospect named variety, challenge and stalled load progression himself. P4c and P4d are partial: the rep established that the plateau exists but never asked what is causing it, and the obvious candidate — the shoulder mobility restriction the prospect had just described — was sitting right there and was never linked to the stalled overhead lifting.

P5.evidence: Entirely absent for the third consecutive call in this batch. No two-year question, no willing-to-settle, no why-not, no line in the sand. The nearest thing is the devil's-advocate challenge, but that is a P4 move about causation and it explicitly did the opposite of a consequence frame — it invited the prospect to articulate that he already gets most of the benefit from what he does now, and then left that on the table. For a 59-year-old whose stated rationale is muscle and core strength as protection against ageing and injury, the cost-of-inaction case writes itself and none of it was made. This is now a settled pattern rather than a lapse: P5 has not run on any call in this batch.

P6.evidence: P6a asked properly and answered cleanly: 'if we're working one-on-one with Trevor to dial in nutrition, training, accountability, do you feel like that's everything that you need to reach that level of mastery?' — 'Yes, absolutely.' P6b was never asked in any form. The rep substituted an unscripted 1-to-10 rating question, which is a good instrument and got a 10 benchmarked against the best coach the prospect has ever worked with, but it measures how good the programme sounds, not whether there is any reason he would not go ahead. That distinction decided the call: the question 'if you had everything you needed, is there any reason you wouldn't go all in on this?' would almost certainly have surfaced both the Ladder contract and the unwillingness to sign the same day, before the price was quoted rather than fifteen minutes after. P6c partial — there was a clear yes on P6a and a 10 out of 10, so moving to price was defensible, but the yes was to the programme, not to proceeding.

P11.evidence: Close attempted — name, billing address, email and phone were captured and the rep asked 'For the investment, you want to do Visa, MasterCard, Amex?' — so the phase applies. Payment refused pending documentation. Steps two to four were unreachable. The rep did the right thing by sharing and reading the agreement live, and then did not convert it: having read the whole contract aloud and having established that the only remaining blockers were a document read and a cancellable $100-a-month app, there was no second attempt at the card and no fallback of any kind. No deposit, no held onboarding slot with Trevor, no booked follow-up call — the prospect left owning the next action entirely.

objection_plays.detail: Trigger: 'let me get back to you at the beginning of the week after this holiday weekend... I wasn't prepared to sign on the bottom line today.' Two of the seven moves ran and both ran well. The belief re-check: 'just quadruple-checking on my end, like, so we are really feeling like, hey, this can be the thing that's going to help you master kettlebells, just to triple-check 100% sure' — answered yes. And the isolate: 'what if you don't mind me asking, what else is coming up that we need to figure out over the weekend?' — answered 'That is it. I just want to take a look at the contract.' That is a textbook isolate and it reduced a deferral to a single, trivial, solvable item. Then the play stopped. No 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is'. No 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?'. No 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now?'. No closing 'are you sure? nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?'. Most costly of all, the rep had the contract open and shared on his own screen and had just read it aloud in full, and did not offer to walk the remaining clauses then and there or ask what specifically the prospect wanted to check. The one thing standing between this call and a close was a document the rep was already displaying.

Recorded because the rep played it when it was not there and was corrected. He characterised the deferral as money — 'So what I'm understanding, I just want to make sure I'm understanding. So we like everything. It's just a matter of like, hey, I wasn't expecting to spend this type of money kind of right now' — and the prospect immediately contradicted him: 'It's really the last thing. Or that, and I wasn't, you know, I wasn't ready to sign on the dotted line because, you know, I got to get out of my ladder contract.' The $6,000 had already been accepted without a beat. Misdiagnosing a documentation objection as a price objection cost momentum at the decisive moment, and the prospect noticed the technique being applied to him: 'you would have been really good at door-to-door. I like how you're handling all the objections.' Scored as a miss on the play rather than dropped, because reaching for the wrong play is a coachable error, not a neutral event.

The most important unanswered objection on the call and it has no script: a free version of the product that is genuinely good enough. The prospect has followed Trevor's free content for years, saves the workouts, picks and chooses push or pull days, and said outright that continuing indefinitely was a live option — 'he puts up enough variety that, again, I could just draft off of him and pick and choose and, you know, forever. And maybe that's what we'll end up doing.' The rep did not respond to that sentence at all. This is a distinct gap from the two already recorded in the playbook: not a cheaper competitor and not a clinical fit problem, but the company's own marketing functioning as a substitute for the company's product. The prospect even handed over the emotional lever to close it — he twice volunteered that he feels guilty about consuming the free work without paying — and that was not used either.

notes: The rep's best discovery of the batch — real reflect-back, a genuine challenge to the prospect's premise, and full transparency on the contract when asked — attached to no consequence frame and no second close. Two specific actions. First, when a prospect names the free content as a viable alternative, treat it as the objection it is; the guilt he volunteered twice was the opening and it was never taken. Second, after an isolate reduces a deferral to one solvable item, close again on that item; here the item was a document the rep already had open and shared. Worth propagating from this call: the 1-to-10 rating question, which produced a benchmarked 10, though it must supplement rather than replace P6b.
